section.title: Solomon's Wisdom
section.sectionRationale: With the throne secured, chapter 3 turns to Solomon's reign itself, opening with a note of compromise, an alliance sealed by marriage to Pharaoh's daughter and worship still offered at the high places because the temple is not yet built. At Gibeon the LORD appears to Solomon in a dream and offers him anything he asks; Solomon, aware of his own inexperience, requests an understanding heart to govern God's people rather than long life, wealth, or victory over his enemies. God grants the request and adds riches and honor besides. The chapter closes with Solomon's famous judgment between two women disputing a living child, proof before all Israel that the wisdom of God was in him.
section.thesis: Solomon's request at Gibeon for an understanding heart, rather than long life, wealth, or vengeance, delights the LORD, who grants him unmatched wisdom along with riches and honor he did not ask for, and that wisdom is immediately displayed before all Israel in a judgment that reveals a true mother's heart and establishes Solomon as a king in whom the wisdom of God visibly dwells.
section.frameNote: Four beats: an uneasy alliance and unfinished worship, verses 1 to 3; Solomon's prayer for an understanding heart at Gibeon, verses 4 to 9; God's answer of wisdom, riches, and honor, verses 10 to 15; and Solomon's judgment between the two women, verses 16 to 28.

verses.text: Later, Solomon formed an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt by marrying his daughter. Solomon brought her to the City of David until he had finished building his palace and the house of the LORD, as well as the wall around Jerusalem.
The people, however, were still sacrificing on the high places because a {{bayit|house}} for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built.
And Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David, except that he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.

units.label: Solomon's prayer for an understanding heart
units.note: ask, and I will give it to you

verses.text: Now the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the great high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar there.
One night at Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream, and God said, “Ask, and I will give it to you!”

Solomon replied, “You have shown much {{chesed|loving devotion}} to Your servant, my father David, because he walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart. And You have maintained this loving devotion by giving him a son to sit on his throne this very day.
And now, O LORD my God, You have made Your servant king in my father David’s place. But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in.
Your servant is here among the people You have chosen, a people too numerous to count or number.
Therefore give Your servant an understanding {{lev|heart}} to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil. For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?”

units.label: God's answer: wisdom, riches, and honor

verses.text: Now it pleased the Lord that Solomon had made this request.

So God said to him, “Since you have asked for this instead of requesting long life or wealth for yourself or death for your enemies, but you have asked for discernment to administer {{mishpat|justice}},
behold, I will do what you have asked. I will give you a wise and discerning heart, so that there will never have been another like you, nor will there ever be.
Moreover, I will give you what you did not request, both riches and honor, so that during all your days no man in any kingdom will be your equal.
So if you walk in My ways and keep My statutes and commandments, just as your father David did, I will prolong your days.”

Then Solomon awoke, and indeed it had been a dream. So he returned to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then he held a feast for all his servants.

units.label: Solomon judges wisely
units.note: the wisdom of God was in him

verses.text: At that time two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.
One woman said, “Please, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth while she was in the house.
On the third day after I gave birth, this woman also had a baby. We were alone, with no one in the house but the two of us.
During the night this woman’s son died because she rolled over on him.
So she got up in the middle of the night and took my son from my side while I was asleep. She laid him in her bosom and put her dead son at my bosom.
The next morning, when I got up to nurse my son, I discovered he was dead. But when I examined him, I realized that he was not the son I had borne.”

“No,” said the other woman, “the living one is my son and the dead one is your son.” But the first woman insisted, “No, the dead one is yours and the living one is mine.” So they argued before the king.
Then the king replied, “This woman says, ‘My son is alive and yours is dead,’ but that woman says, ‘No, your son is dead and mine is alive.’”
The king continued, “Bring me a sword.” So they brought him a sword,
and the king declared, “Cut the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other.”

Then the woman whose son was alive spoke to the king because she yearned with compassion for her son. “Please, my lord,” she said, “give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” But the other woman said, “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!”
Then the king gave his ruling: “Give the living baby to the first woman. By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.”
When all Israel heard of the judgment the king had given, they stood in awe of him, for they saw that the {{chokmah|wisdom}} of God was in him to administer {{mishpat|justice}}.

bayit.gloss: House, here specifically the house, or temple, for the Name of the LORD, not yet built when Solomon prays at Gibeon. The people still sacrifice at scattered high places because this bayit does not yet exist; its construction, filling the chapters ahead, will finally give Israel one central place to meet with God, a shadow of the true dwelling of God with His people fulfilled in Christ, John 1:14, and in the church, His body, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant kindness. Solomon opens his prayer by recounting the chesed the LORD has already shown his father David, and the chesed maintained in giving David a son to sit on his throne. His request for wisdom grows directly out of gratitude for grace already received, not merit he has earned.

lev.gloss: Heart, the seat of understanding, discernment, and moral character. Solomon asks for an understanding lev to judge God's people rightly, echoing 1 Samuel 16:7, where the LORD looks on the lev rather than outward appearance. Wisdom, in Scripture, is finally a matter of the heart, not merely the intellect.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of a case or a society according to God's standards. Solomon asks for discernment to administer mishpat, and the chapter closes by showing that very mishpat displayed before all Israel in the case of the two women, proof that the LORD had granted exactly what Solomon requested.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, skill in living rightly before God and administering His justice well. This is the chapter's central word: it is what Solomon asks for above riches or long life, what God grants beyond all others, and what all Israel finally recognizes at work in him, 'the chokmah of God was in him.' Christ is greater than Solomon and is Himself the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, 30, Matthew 12:42.

basic.context: Chapter 3 opens with a note of compromise, an alliance sealed by marriage to Pharaoh's daughter and worship still offered at the high places since the temple is not yet built. At Gibeon the LORD appears to Solomon in a dream and offers him anything he asks; Solomon requests an understanding heart to govern God's people rather than long life, wealth, or the death of his enemies. God is pleased and grants the request, adding riches and honor Solomon did not ask for. The chapter closes with Solomon's famous ruling between two women disputing a living child, a judgment that leaves all Israel in awe at the wisdom of God at work in him. The key questions are what Solomon's request reveals about true wisdom, why God gives so generously beyond what was asked, and how the case of the two women demonstrates that wisdom in action.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing a real dream encounter and a real legal case, not a formula guaranteeing that anyone who asks for wisdom receives supernatural insight in the same measure. What the chapter teaches as an enduring truth is that God delights in requests shaped by love for others rather than self-interest, and that true wisdom flows from a heart rightly ordered toward Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The people still lack a bayit, a house, for the LORD's Name, so Solomon worships at Gibeon instead. There he asks for an understanding lev, heart, to govern well, and God grants him chokmah, wisdom, beyond any other, along with the mishpat, justice, that Israel then sees displayed in his famous ruling.
basic.typology: Solomon's request for wisdom rather than riches or long life anticipates Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. God's generosity in giving Solomon more than he asked pictures the Father's pattern of giving immeasurably more than we ask or imagine. And Solomon's discerning judgment, exposing the true mother's heart, points to Christ, who perfectly discerns the true condition of every heart.
basic.christ: Solomon asks for wisdom to govern rightly and receives it as an unearned gift; Jesus is greater than Solomon, and is Himself the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:30, Matthew 12:42. Where Solomon's wisdom was given and could later be compromised, Christ's wisdom is perfect, unfailing, and freely offered to all who ask, James 1:5.
basic.god: God delights in prayers shaped by love for others rather than self-interest, and He gives generously, often far beyond what is asked. He is also the God of true justice, whose wisdom is displayed not in abstract theory but in real, costly discernment applied to real human need.
basic.crossReferences: James 1:5 promises that God gives wisdom generously to all who ask. 1 Kings 4:29-34 describes the astonishing breadth of the wisdom God gave Solomon. Matthew 12:42 records Jesus declaring that something greater than Solomon is here. And 1 Corinthians 1:30 names Christ Himself as our wisdom from God.
basic.oneStory: Israel now has a king, but not yet a temple, and in that unfinished season God meets Solomon in a dream and gives him what he asked, wisdom to govern well. That wisdom is displayed immediately and becomes the hallmark of Solomon's early reign, a foretaste of the true wisdom of God finally and fully revealed in Jesus, greater than Solomon, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a frame around its own center. It opens by naming what Solomon does not yet have, a house for the LORD, and a foreign wife brought into an unfinished city, verses 1 to 3, and it closes with what Solomon undeniably has, the wisdom of God recognized by ordinary people in an impossible case, verse 28. Between those two brackets sits the dream at Gibeon, told entirely as dialogue, God's one open question, ask, and I will give it to you, verse 5, and Solomon's long, self-effacing answer, verses 6 to 9, followed by God's own longer answer that both grants the specific request and multiplies it, verses 11 to 14.

The courtroom scene that follows is deliberately theatrical. The narrator lets both women speak at length, in nearly identical, mirrored claims, the living one is my son, no, the dead one is yours and the living one is mine, verse 23, so that the reader is left as stuck as the king before he calls for a sword. Only the test itself, not any evidence, breaks the deadlock. This staging turns what could have been reported in a single sentence, Solomon judged wisely, into a scene long enough that the wisdom just granted in the dream is demonstrated rather than merely declared.
context.historical:
Gibeon lay some six miles northwest of Jerusalem, in territory belonging to Benjamin, and it was already a place heavy with history by Solomon's day. Centuries earlier its inhabitants had tricked Joshua into an oath of protection, Joshua 9:3-15, and Saul's later slaughter of Gibeonites in violation of that same oath brought a three-year famine on Israel that David had to answer for, 2 Samuel 21:1-2. That the LORD chooses this particular city, once wronged by an earlier king, to bless Saul's replacement dynasty so richly is a detail easy to miss but hard to think accidental.

Royal dream encounters at a sanctuary were not unheard of in the ancient world; kings elsewhere in the Near East likewise sought guidance through sleeping at a shrine. What sets this scene apart is not the setting but its content. Solomon is offered anything without condition, ask, and I will give it to you, and answers not with a request for personal advantage but with a confession of his own inexperience as a little child, verse 7, unusual candor for a king only recently secured on his throne by the executions of the previous chapter.

The case of the two women also reflects a real gap in ancient legal procedure. With no midwife, witness, or record to consult, and both claimants equally without a husband to vouch for them, the court had no evidence to weigh, only the mothers' competing claims, which is exactly why the case became famous as proof of wisdom rather than mere legal skill.
context.canonical:
Solomon's plea, who is able to govern this great people of Yours, verse 9, echoes a much older cry. Moses himself, worn out trying to judge Israel alone, was told by Jethro that the burden was too heavy for one man, Exodus 18:17-18, and the solution then was delegation, appointing judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Solomon does not ask to delegate; he asks to be equipped, and the LORD answers by giving one man what an entire tier of judges once supplied.

The chapter also plants seeds that the rest of Kings will make grow. The marriage alliance and the worship on the high places, verses 1 to 3, look almost incidental here, excused twice as a matter of the temple not yet being built, yet by 1 Kings 11:1-8 the reader learns that Solomon's foreign marriages and his toleration of high places for foreign gods will be named as the very cause of the kingdom's later tearing. What reads here as understandable compromise becomes, read across the whole book, an early warning the narrator lets stand without comment.

Later Scripture treats Solomon's wisdom as a settled fact worth citing rather than a private legend; the Queen of Sheba travels a great distance to test it, 1 Kings 10:1-9, and Jesus Himself assumes His hearers already know the story well enough to be measured against it, Matthew 12:42.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants Israel, and every later reader who ever ruled or served under a ruler, to see what kind of asking pleases God. Solomon is given complete freedom, ask, and I will give it to you, and his answer becomes a small window into character, not a grasp for security or vengeance, but an admission of his own limits and a request shaped entirely around the needs of the people he must serve. The author means for that pattern of prayer, self-aware, others-centered, rooted in gratitude for grace already shown, to be recognized as itself a mark of the wisdom being requested.

The author also intends the courtroom scene to answer a hidden question the dream leaves open, whether the gift was real. By showing wisdom solve an unsolvable case with no evidence at all, the narrator lets the reader, and all Israel, verse 28, judge the answer to the prayer for themselves rather than merely being told about it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter reports one particular dream, one particular case, and one particular king's particular compromises; it is not a pattern guaranteeing dreams as the normal channel of divine wisdom or endorsing the threat of a sword as legal technique. Believers are not meant to seek visions at ancient shrines or stage similar tests in modern courts.

What the chapter does establish as abiding truth is the shape of a prayer God delights to answer and the shape wisdom takes once granted, self-forgetful in what it asks, decisive and compassionate in what it does. It also quietly teaches that partial obedience, worship at the high places because the temple was not yet built, can coexist for a season with real devotion without yet being corrected, though Scripture will not let that arrangement stand forever.

debates.question: Why does God grant Solomon far more than he requested, riches and honor alongside wisdom?

views.label: A reward tied to the unselfishness of the request itself
views.case: Verses 11 to 13 explicitly list what Solomon refused to ask for, long life, wealth, the death of his enemies, before naming what God grants beyond the request, suggesting the added gifts are a direct response to the very shape of Solomon's asking.

views.label: Unconditional grace, distinct from the one conditional promise
views.case: Verse 14 alone attaches a condition, if you walk in My ways, to the promise of long life, while riches and honor in verse 13 carry no such condition, suggesting these gifts are simply free grace rather than payment for a well-phrased prayer.

debates.bearing: The text itself draws this line: verses 13 and 14 separate the unconditional grants from the single conditional promise, so wisdom and blessing beyond it are pure gift, even while persevering in that gift still calls for an obedient, walking life.

debates.question: Does the narrator approve of Solomon's worship at Gibeon and the high places, or merely report it with quiet caution?

views.label: A legitimate arrangement for its moment
views.case: The text excuses the practice twice, verses 2 and 3, as provisional given the temple's absence, and Gibeon specifically housed the LORD's own tabernacle and altar at the time, 1 Chronicles 21:29, so this need not be read as pagan worship at all.

views.label: A detail placed here as an early warning
views.case: The note is phrased as an exception to Solomon's love for the LORD, except that he sacrificed on the high places, and the phrase high places becomes, within a few chapters of Kings, shorthand for exactly the syncretism that ruins later kings, so its neutral appearance here may be more ominous than it first looks.

debates.bearing: Most careful readers hold both together, legitimate for its own moment, yet the narrator's later use of high places as a recurring danger suggests the detail is placed here deliberately rather than as background filler.

study.originalLanguages:
Solomon's famous request in verse 9 is, word for word, not quite an understanding heart but lev shomea, a hearing heart, or a heart that listens. The verb shama, to hear, runs through the whole of Deuteronomy's call to obedience, Hear, O Israel, Deuteronomy 6:4, and by asking for a heart that hears, Solomon asks less for cleverness than for a heart trained to actually listen, to evidence, to people, and ultimately to God, before it renders judgment.

He calls himself a na'ar qatan, verse 7, a little child, or young man, the same phrase used of David himself as a shepherd boy, 1 Samuel 17:33, and elsewhere of servants far too inexperienced to be trusted with weighty responsibility. Solomon is almost certainly not literally a boy, he has just executed several men in the previous chapter, but the phrase is a deliberate confession of inadequacy rather than a statement about his actual age.

Verse 3 says Solomon ahav, loved, the LORD, the same verb Deuteronomy uses for Israel's whole duty, love the LORD your God with all your heart, Deuteronomy 6:5, and the same verb this very chapter's book will use again of Solomon's fondness for foreign women, 1 Kings 11:1. The narrator plants the word early, in its right and best sense, so that its later, disordered use becomes unmistakable by contrast.

God speaks to Solomon in a chalom, a dream, verse 5, the same word used of Joseph's dreams in Genesis 37 and of Jacob's ladder at Bethel, Genesis 28:12, a recognized but relatively rare vehicle of revelation in Scripture, reserved for pivotal moments rather than everyday guidance.

The chapter's five lexicon terms trace Solomon's whole transaction with God. He lacks a bayit, house, for the Name; he appeals to the chesed already shown his father; he asks for a lev fit to hear rightly; God grants him chokmah beyond measure; and all Israel finally recognizes that chokmah operating as mishpat, justice, in a hard case. Every major noun in the chapter, house, loyalty, heart, wisdom, justice, belongs to a single unbroken argument, because God had already been faithful, Solomon can ask rightly, and because he asked rightly, God's wisdom becomes visible to an entire nation.

Numbers 12:6-8 ranks dream revelation as real but lesser than the LORD's direct, mouth to mouth speech reserved uniquely for Moses, a detail that quietly tempers how much weight the original audience would have placed on the form of this encounter, a chalom rather than a clearer word, even while never doubting that the message it carried was genuine.

typology.type: Solomon confessing he is only a na'ar qatan, a little child, unable to judge without help, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: Moses made the same confession at the burning bush, who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, Exodus 3:11, and both men were answered not by having their weakness removed but by being given a resource, God's presence for Moses, wisdom for Solomon, that made the weakness beside the point. Christ reverses the pattern from the far side; He alone among all who have ever ruled needed to confess no inadequacy, in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom, Colossians 2:3, the completed answer every self-confessed little child, including Solomon, was only ever pointing toward.

typology.type: God's unconditioned generosity, granting wisdom and adding riches and honor Solomon never requested, verses 12-13
typology.fulfillment: The chapter's extravagance, giving far beyond the ask, anticipates a pattern Paul later names outright, that God is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, Ephesians 3:20. Solomon's unrequested riches were real but temporary, gone within a few generations to a foreign treasury; the far greater gift given in Christ, an inheritance that can never perish, spoil, or fade, 1 Peter 1:4, does not depend on a king's own uncertain heart to preserve it.

typology.type: Solomon's proposed sword exposing which woman truly loved the child, verses 24-27
typology.fulfillment: The test does not harm the child; it simply makes hidden love visible by what each woman was willing to lose. Hebrews describes the word of God working the same way on a larger scale, sharper than any two-edged sword, discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart, Hebrews 4:12, exposing what people truly love long before any actual harm is threatened. Solomon's test was a single clever ruse for a single case; Christ's discernment reaches every heart, and unlike Solomon's sword, it never needs to bluff.

study.christ:
Solomon's own confession, that he does not know how to go out or come in, verse 7, sets up a contrast the rest of Scripture will not let the reader miss. Isaiah describes the coming Branch of David as one on whom will rest the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, who will not judge by what His eyes see but with perfect righteousness, Isaiah 11:2-4, precisely the discernment Solomon can only ask for rather than possess natively. Where Solomon needed a dream to be equipped for one hard case, Jesus says of Himself, I can do nothing on My own; I judge only as I hear, John 5:30, a hearing that is not granted once at Gibeon but is continuous and complete.

The courtroom scene also points to Christ by a striking reversal. The false mother is willing to see the living child divided so that neither of them will have him whole; true love, the narrator shows, refuses division even at great personal cost, give her the living baby, do not kill him, verse 26. At the cross that logic runs the other way entirely. Christ Himself is the one who is divided, His body broken for His people, so that His people need not be. Where the true mother in Solomon's court would rather lose her claim than see her son harmed, Christ actually bears the harm Himself so that those who are His are not lost.

Solomon's wisdom also draws its own limits into the light. It could resolve one hard case in public, but it could not keep his own heart from later drifting after foreign gods, 1 Kings 11:4. A wisdom that fails its own possessor cannot be the final answer to what ails a people. The New Testament names one who succeeds where Solomon's wisdom eventually failed, calling Himself, without qualification, greater than Solomon, Matthew 12:42, not because He received more wisdom than Solomon did, but because He is Himself the wisdom by which the world was made, 1 Corinthians 1:24, a wisdom that never needs a second gift to keep it whole.
study.god:
Notice how the text names God in this scene. The LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream, and God said, ask, verse 5, moving in one sentence from the covenant name to the more general title. The shift is subtle but consistent with how this book speaks throughout; the LORD is the personal, promise-keeping name, God the more universal title for the one all people must reckon with. Both are true of the same being who meets Solomon that night, at once Israel's covenant LORD and sovereign over every nation whose kings will later come to hear Solomon speak.

God's evaluation in this scene weighs absence as carefully as presence. Verse 11 lists three things Solomon did not ask for, long life, wealth, the death of his enemies, before it ever states what he did ask for. That is a striking way to describe divine pleasure, God reading Solomon's heart not only by what filled his prayer but by what he left out of it, refusing to grasp for the very things kings normally seize first.

God's generosity here is not indiscriminate. Riches and honor are given outright, no strings attached, verse 13, but length of days is explicitly conditioned, if you walk in My ways, verse 14. The chapter therefore refuses two easy caricatures of God at once, a stingy deity who rewards nothing freely, and an indulgent one who ties nothing to obedience. Some gifts are simply given; others remain bound to a life still being lived faithfully, and Solomon's own later history will show exactly why that condition mattered.

Finally, God is shown willing to let His gift be tested in public before it is trusted. He does not merely tell Solomon in private that wisdom has been granted; He lets that wisdom be proven in an open, desperate case with two women and a sword, so that an entire nation, not only a king, can see for itself what God has done, verse 28.

crossReferences.note: Centuries before Solomon's dream, Gibeon's people tricked Joshua into a sworn treaty of protection rather than face Israel's conquest honestly. That old, binding oath still stood in Solomon's day. It is a striking detail that God chooses to bless a new king so richly at the very city whose people once had to survive Israel by deception rather than by combat.

Saul's slaughter of the Gibeonites, breaking Israel's ancient oath to them, brought a three-year famine that David had to resolve by handing over seven of Saul's descendants. Solomon's rich blessing at Gibeon, a single generation later, quietly answers that older, bloody history with a scene of abundant, undeserved favor instead.

Jethro warns Moses that judging Israel alone will wear him out and the people out with him, urging him to share the burden among appointed judges. Solomon's cry, who is able to govern this great people, echoes the same exhaustion, but his answer is not delegation; it is a heart made sufficient by God for the task Moses could not carry alone.

Moses had already warned that Israel's king must not acquire many horses, wives, or silver and gold, but must instead copy out the law for himself and read it daily. Solomon's chapter-opening marriage alliance and worship at the high places sit uneasily beside this old warning, a tension the narrator lets stand rather than resolve.

Solomon's many foreign wives eventually turn his heart after other gods, and he builds high places for their idols. The marriage and worship noted almost in passing here return in this later chapter as the explicit cause of the kingdom's later tearing, proof that Scripture lets small compromises grow visible consequences.

The Queen of Sheba travels a great distance specifically to test Solomon's reported wisdom with hard questions, and comes away declaring that even the reports she had heard did not tell the half of it. Her visit is the wider world's own verdict on the very gift first granted quietly in a dream at Gibeon.

The word of God is described as living, active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Solomon used an actual sword to expose one hidden heart in a single hard case; the writer of Hebrews describes a discernment that reaches every heart, always, without needing any prop at all.

Paul says that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Solomon's wisdom, however vast, was borrowed and eventually compromised by his own divided heart; the wisdom Paul describes is not granted to Christ from outside but belongs to Him as who He is, the far greater fulfillment of everything Solomon's gift only pictured.

Paul praises the God who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine. Solomon experienced exactly this kind of overflow, riches and honor added to a request that never mentioned them, a pattern of divine generosity that culminates, for those in Christ, in blessings no earthly court could ever calculate.

James promises that God gives wisdom generously to anyone who asks, without finding fault. Solomon's dream at Gibeon is the Old Testament's own proof of exactly this promise centuries before James wrote it, a king who asked honestly and was answered without being shamed for admitting his own inadequacy.

study.oneStory:
The oldest temptation in Scripture promised knowledge of good and evil as something to be seized, you will be like God, knowing good and evil, Genesis 3:5, grasped by theft rather than given by grace. Solomon's prayer asks for exactly that same discernment, to discern between good and evil, verse 9, yet asks for it as a gift rather than taking it as a right, and receives from God's own hand what humanity's first parents tried to take from His tree. The whole of this chapter can be read as one small but real reversal of Eden's original grasping.

That reversal bears fruit across the rest of the Old Testament's wisdom literature. Proverbs opens by declaring that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, Proverbs 1:7, the same posture Solomon models at Gibeon, an admitted need answered by a God who gives rather than a secret pried loose by cunning. Solomon becomes, in Israel's later memory, the chief voice of exactly this kind of wisdom, composing proverbs and songs that shape how God's people think about ordinary life under God long after his throne is gone, 1 Kings 4:32.

Yet this chapter's own honesty will not let the reversal be called complete. The same king who asks so well at Gibeon will, within a few chapters, begin loving foreign women in a way Deuteronomy had already warned against, and by 1 Kings 11 his heart will be turned after their gods. The gift of wisdom did not, by itself, guarantee a wise life lived to the end.

The story therefore keeps moving forward, past Solomon, in search of a wisdom that will not eventually be compromised by the very heart that received it. It finds its rest in Christ, who is not merely wise but is Himself the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, the one in whom the ancient hunger for the knowledge of good and evil is finally satisfied rightly, by grace, without ever curdling into another Eden.

sermon.title: A King's Wisdom, Solomon
sermon.why: Preached from 1 Kings 3:16-28 as part of the series Pointers to Christ, Keller examines the need for wisdom, the anatomy of wisdom, and the heart of wisdom running through Solomon's judgment, directly expounding this chapter's climactic scene.

quiz.q: What did Solomon ask God for at Gibeon, and what did he deliberately not ask for?

options.text: He asked for an understanding heart to discern good and evil and govern God's people rightly, deliberately not asking for long life, wealth, or the death of his enemies, v9, 11.
options.note: Verses 9 and 11 together state exactly this request and its deliberate exclusions.

options.text: He asked to be a good king like his father David, without making any specific request.
options.note: Too vague; the prayer contains a specific, named request, an understanding heart to discern and to judge.

options.text: He asked mainly for wealth and honor so that his reign would be secure.
options.note: The opposite of what he requested; wealth and honor were explicitly what he did not ask for, though God granted them anyway, verse 13.

options.text: He asked for victory over all his enemies.
options.note: Explicitly not requested and contrary to verse 11, which lists this among the things Solomon did not ask for.

quiz.q: Why did it please the Lord that Solomon made this request, verses 10-12?

options.text: Because Solomon asked for discernment to administer justice rather than for personal gain, self-preservation, or vengeance.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly contrasts Solomon's actual request with the self-serving requests he could have made.

options.text: Because Solomon prayed at all, simply showing that he still trusted God despite his youth.
options.note: True but partial; it understates the specific, others-focused content of the request that the text highlights.

options.text: Because Solomon promised to build the temple immediately as part of his prayer.
options.note: Not part of the recorded prayer at Gibeon; the temple's construction is addressed in later chapters.

options.text: Because Solomon asked for something small and unimportant.
options.note: Contrary to the text, which repeatedly treats this request as significant and worthy of God's pleasure.

quiz.q: What did God give Solomon beyond what he requested?

options.text: Riches and honor, so that no king in his lifetime would equal him, in addition to the wise and discerning heart he had asked for.
options.note: Verses 12-13 state this precisely.

options.text: Only long life, since that is what most kings desire above all else.
options.note: Long life is mentioned in verse 14, but it is conditional on obedience and is not the primary unrequested gift highlighted in verses 12-13.

options.text: Nothing further; God gave Solomon exactly what he asked and no more.
options.note: Contrary to verse 13, which explicitly states God gave what Solomon did not request.

options.text: Victory over Egypt as a reward for his faithfulness.
options.note: Not in the text, and Solomon had just made a marriage alliance with Egypt, verse 1, not fought against it.

quiz.q: How does Solomon's judgment between the two women reveal true wisdom, verses 16-27?

options.text: By proposing to divide the living child, Solomon exposes which woman truly loves the child by her willingness to give him up rather than see him harmed.
options.note: Verses 26-27 show the test revealing the true mother's compassion, which becomes the basis for Solomon's ruling.

options.text: By carefully cross-examining both women's stories for factual inconsistencies.
options.note: The text shows no cross-examination of details; the decisive test is the proposal to divide the child, not detective work on their stories.

options.text: By ruling in favor of whichever woman spoke first and most confidently.
options.note: The ruling depends on the compassion revealed under the sword test, not on who spoke first or most confidently.

options.text: By actually dividing the child in two as he first proposed.
options.note: That proposal was a test, not the actual judgment; verse 27 shows the living child given whole to his true mother.

quiz.q: What was Israel's response to Solomon's ruling, and what did the narrator say it proved?

options.text: All Israel stood in awe of the king because they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.
options.note: This is the exact closing statement of the chapter, verse 28.

options.text: The two women reconciled with each other and became close friends.
options.note: Not stated anywhere in the text; the narrative closes with Israel's response to Solomon, not the women's relationship.

options.text: The people demanded that a formal written law be created based on the case.
options.note: Not mentioned in the text.

options.text: The people were unimpressed, believing the ruling was merely a lucky guess.
options.note: The opposite of verse 28, which says the people stood in awe, recognizing God's own wisdom at work.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: Solomon's wisdom, sought and given as a gift rather than earned, anticipates Christ, who is Himself the wisdom of God and greater than Solomon.
options.note: Directly supported by 1 Corinthians 1:30 and Jesus's own words in Matthew 12:42.

options.text: It shows that good kings always ask God for help before making any decision.
options.note: True in a general sense, but it understates the specific, christological pointer the chapter contains.

options.text: It teaches that wisdom can only be gained through many years of hard experience.
options.note: Contrary to the chapter, where Solomon's wisdom is a sudden gift given while he is still, by his own admission, only 'a little child,' verse 7.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to Christ or the New Testament.
options.note: False; the connection is explicit in Jesus's own statement that something greater than Solomon is here, Matthew 12:42.

questions: Solomon could have asked for long life, wealth, or victory over his enemies, but asked instead for wisdom to serve others well. If God offered you anything right now, what would your request reveal about your heart?
God delighted in Solomon's request because it was shaped by love for God's people rather than self-interest. Where in your own praying do you notice self-interest crowding out love for others?
God gave Solomon far more than he asked for. Where have you seen God's generosity exceed what you dared to request, and how does that shape your confidence in bringing requests to Him now?
The chapter opens with Solomon's compromise at the high places even as it celebrates his wisdom. Where might you be tempted to accept partial obedience alongside genuine devotion to God?

Solomon's wisdom was tested and proven in a real, costly, human situation, not in the abstract. Where is God currently asking you to apply wisdom to a real and difficult situation rather than simply admiring wisdom from a distance?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote observes that 'the Lord' here and in verse 15 renders the Hebrew Adonai, distinct from the covenant name LORD, YHWH, used elsewhere in the chapter.

The narrator's note that the people, and even Solomon, sacrificed at the high places 'because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built' softens the practice as a provisional necessity rather than deliberate idolatry, though it still plants an early seed that resurfaces later in Solomon's reign, 1 Kings 11:7-8.

The two women are identified as prostitutes, a detail that heightens the difficulty of the case, since neither had a husband or independent witness to support her claim, making Solomon's discernment all the more remarkable.
